opus-5.5.text:
I think data quality is honestly one of the most underappreciated parts of the whole process. People tend to focus on model architecture or the sheer amount of compute, and those matter, but what the model actually learns is shaped very directly by what you feed it.

In the early days of scaling, the mindset was more or less "more data is better." What we've learned since is that the composition and quality of that data matter enormously. If you have a lot of noisy, repetitive, or low-value text, the model spends capacity learning things you don't actually want. If you curate carefully, removing duplicates, filtering out low-quality content, and balancing across domains like code, math, science, and multiple languages, you get a model that's much more capable for the same amount of compute.

With a model like Gemini, which is multimodal from the ground up, this gets even more interesting. It's not just text quality anymore. You have to think about how well images, video, and audio are aligned with the text that describes them. If the pairing is weak or inaccurate, the model learns the wrong associations. So a lot of work goes into making sure the different modalities actually correspond to each other in meaningful ways.

Then there's the post-training side, where quality matters perhaps even more. When you're doing instruction tuning or learning from human feedback, a relatively small amount of very high-quality data can shift the model's behavior a lot. A few thousand excellent examples can be worth more than millions of mediocre ones. So we invest a lot in clear guidelines for raters, in checking consistency, and in making sure the examples reflect the behavior we actually want, like being helpful, accurate, and safe.

And increasingly, models themselves are part of the data pipeline. We use models to help filter, score, and even generate training data. That's powerful, but it also means you need very good evaluation to make sure you're not just amplifying the model's own mistakes.

So if I had to summarize: compute and architecture set the ceiling, but data quality largely determines how close you get to it.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture and compute matter, but the data the model learns from shapes its capability and data quality determines how close it gets to its potential.

r002.rationale: The response discusses training-data composition and curation, but does not say that model papers generally withhold training-data details.

fable-5.1.text:
Data quality is, honestly, one of the things I'd put right at the top of the list. People tend to focus on architecture or on scaling compute, and those matter, but in my experience the model is only ever as good as what you feed it. If the data is noisy, redundant, or subtly wrong, you end up spending enormous amounts of compute learning things you'd rather the model didn't learn, and then trying to undo that later with post-training.

With something like Gemini 2.0, a lot of the work that doesn't get talked about is the unglamorous part: filtering, deduplication, deciding how to weight different sources, figuring out which data actually improves the capabilities you care about versus just adding volume. And it's not a one-time decision. As the model gets more capable, your notion of "high quality" shifts too. Data that was useful early on can become something the model has essentially saturated, and the question becomes what's the next thing that teaches it something new.

The other piece is that quality means different things depending on the goal. For reasoning, you want data where the steps are actually correct and well-explained, not just the final answer. For multimodal work, alignment between the modalities matters a lot. For code, you care about whether it actually runs. So "data quality" isn't a single knob, it's a whole set of judgments, and those judgments end up shaping the model's personality and strengths as much as anything else in the pipeline.

r001.rationale: It says architecture and compute matter, but the model is only as good as its data, so those resources alone do not ensure a very good model.

r002.rationale: It says some data work does not get talked about, but does not say model papers generally withhold details about their training data.

astra-6.text:
I think data quality is foundational. It’s easy to focus on how much data you have, but what matters is what the model can learn from it. Is it accurate? Is it relevant? Does it cover the range of situations where you want the model to be useful?

For a model like Gemini 2.0, that question also spans different types of data. With text, images, audio, and video, you care about the quality of each modality, but also whether they line up meaningfully. Does the text actually describe what’s happening in the image or video?

And quality isn’t just about filtering out bad examples. It’s also about preserving diversity. If you filter too aggressively, you can lose unusual but valuable examples. So the goal is to give the model reliable learning signals while still representing the breadth of what it will encounter.

r001.rationale: The response calls data quality foundational but does not mention model architecture or GPU resources, or challenge the idea that they alone ensure a very good model.

r002.rationale: The response discusses data quality and modalities but does not observe that model papers generally withhold training data details.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data quality is fundamental. It’s tempting to focus on how much data you have, but you also have to ask: Is it accurate? Is it useful? And does it cover the kinds of situations where you want the model to perform well?

For a model like Gemini 2.0, that question extends across modalities. You care about the quality of the text, images, audio, and video, but also how those pieces relate to one another. If the relationships are noisy, that makes learning harder.

And quality doesn’t simply mean keeping only polished, textbook-style examples. You need diversity, too—different ways people express themselves, different contexts, and difficult cases. The challenge is to reduce unhelpful noise without losing that breadth. So I’d think of data quality as an ongoing process of curation, evaluation, and understanding where the model still needs better examples.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes data quality, diversity, and curation, but does not address whether architecture and GPU resources alone ensure a very good model.
